title: Roughness Exponent H vs Measurement Bias Scaling
mathematical_formulation:
Bias(H; instrument) = B_0 · (f_inst / f_ref)^(2H-2)

where:
  Bias = (σ_measured² - σ_true²) / σ_true²
  f_inst = instrument cutoff frequency
  f_ref = reference high-frequency limit

For stylus: Bias_s ∝ r_tip^(1-H) · σ^(H-1)
For optical: Bias_o ∝ (λ/NA)^(2-2H) · σ^(2H-1)

Crossover condition (Bias_s = Bias_o):
  r_tip / (λ/NA) = (λ/NA / σ)^((1-2H)/(1-H))
physical_interpretation: The bias in measured roughness depends critically on the surface's Hurst exponent H. For smooth surfaces (H → 1), both instruments approach the true roughness. For rough surfaces (H → 0), the bias becomes severe and instrument-dependent. This provides a rigorous criterion for when stylus and optical measurements can be compared: they agree only when both resolve all roughness scales, which requires f_inst ≫ 1/L_c.
testable_prediction: For H = 0.3 (fractal-like rough surface): Bias_s and Bias_o can differ by > 50% even when both instruments are 'well-calibrated'. For H = 0.9 (smooth): bias is negligible (< 5%) for both. This is testable on calibration gratings with known H.

title: Spectral Information Loss Field I(f_x, f_y)
mathematical_formulation:
I(f_x, f_y) = log₁₀[ PSD_true(f_x, f_y) / PSD_measured(f_x, f_y) ]

Integrated information loss: L = ∫∫ I(f_x, f_y) df_x df_y

Per-band information loss: L_band = ∫_{band} I(f_x, f_y) df_x df_y

Properties:
  • I(f_x, f_y) ≥ 0 (measurement never adds information)
  • I(f_x, f_y) = 0 in the passband
  • I(f_x, f_y) → ∞ at the instrument cutoff
  • I conveys more than RMSE: two systems with identical RMSE can have different I(f_x, f_y) distributions
physical_interpretation: I(f_x, f_y) is a 2D map showing where in k-space each instrument loses information about the true surface. This is fundamentally different from RMSE, which collapses all spatial-frequency information into a single scalar. I(f_x, f_y) reveals anisotropic loss patterns — e.g. stylus loses more along the scan direction due to tip convolution, while optical loses isotropically at the diffraction limit.
testable_prediction: For a known test surface (e.g. sinusoidal grating), I(f_x, f_y) can be measured directly and compared to the theoretical H_sensor(f_x, f_y). The integrated loss L should scale with r_tip/λ_dominant for stylus and λ_dominant·NA/λ for optical.

title: Measurement Anisotropy Tensor A_ij
mathematical_formulation:
A_ij = ∫∫ f_i f_j · H_sensor(f_x, f_y) · df_x df_y  /  ∫∫ H_sensor(f_x, f_y) df_x df_y

where f_1 = f_x, f_2 = f_y

Eigendecomposition: A = λ_1 ê_1 ê_1^T + λ_2 ê_2 ê_2^T

Anisotropy degree: α = |λ_1 - λ_2| / (λ_1 + λ_2)
Anisotropy direction: θ_A = arctan(ê_1,y / ê_1,x)

For perfect isotropic sensor: A_ij ∝ δ_ij, α = 0
For stylus (raster along x): A_xx > A_yy, α > 0, θ_A ≈ 0° or 90°
For optical (circular aperture): A_ij ≈ A_0 δ_ij, α ≈ 0
physical_interpretation: The anisotropy tensor A_ij quantifies the directional dependence of measurement fidelity. Its eigenvalues λ_1, λ_2 give the principal bandwidths, and its eigenvectors ê_1, ê_2 give the directions of maximum and minimum information transmission. α = 0 means isotropic measurement; α = 1 means purely 1D measurement (e.g. single profilometer trace). This provides a rigorous, coordinate-invariant characterisation of measurement anisotropy.
testable_prediction: For a stylus instrument scanning along x: α_stylus > 0.5 (highly anisotropic). For a WLI with NA=0.55: α_optical < 0.05 (nearly isotropic). The product α · L (anisotropy × loss) is a dimensionless figure of merit.

title: Unified k-Space Measurement Operator for Surface Profilometry
mathematical_formulation:
M[h(x,y)] = F^{-1}[ H(f_x, f_y) · F[h(x,y)] ] + η(x,y)

where H(f_x, f_y) = H_aperture(f_x, f_y) · H_sampling(f_x, f_y) · H_noise(f_x, f_y)

For stylus: H_s(f_x, f_y) = sinc(π f_x Δx) · sinc(π f_y Δy) · exp(-2π²σ_tip²(f_x² + f_y²))
For optical: H_o(f_x, f_y) = circ(√(f_x²+f_y²) · λ/NA) · exp(-σ_phase²(f_x, f_y))

Ratio operator: R(f_x, f_y) = H_o(f_x, f_y) / H_s(f_x, f_y)
physical_interpretation: Every surface measurement can be represented as a linear operator acting on the true height field h(x,y), followed by additive noise η. The transfer function H(f_x, f_y) encapsulates the instrument's k-space filtering. The stylus acts as a low-pass filter with tip-radius-dependent Gaussian roll-off plus raster sampling sinc modulation. The optical system has a hard circular cutoff at the diffraction limit plus phase-noise-dependent degradation.
testable_prediction: For surfaces with roughness below the optical diffraction limit but above the stylus tip-radius cutoff, the ratio R(f_x, f_y) should show a cross-over region where R ≈ 1 (equivalence regime), flanked by regions where one modality dominates.

title: Tip-Radius Cutoff Scaling Law
mathematical_formulation:
f_c(r_tip, H, σ) = C · r_tip^(-β) · σ^(γ) · L_c^(H-1)

where:
  f_c = effective cutoff spatial frequency
  r_tip = stylus tip radius
  H = surface Hurst exponent
  σ = RMS roughness
  L_c = correlation length
  β ≈ 0.5 (theoretical: f_c ∝ 1/√r_tip for Gaussian tip approximation)
  γ = H - 1 (roughness-dependent correction)

In dimensionless form: f_c* = C · (L_c/r_tip)^β · (σ/L_c)^γ
physical_interpretation: The effective spatial-frequency cutoff of a stylus instrument scales as f_c ∝ r_tip^(-1/2), not r_tip^(-1) as naive intuition suggests. This is because the tip acts as a morphological filter whose width in k-space is set by the tip's radius of curvature convolved with the surface's curvature distribution. The Hurst exponent H enters because smoother surfaces (higher H) have less high-curvature asperities, effectively increasing the cutoff for a given tip radius.
testable_prediction: For a self-affine surface with H = 0.7: plotting log(f_c) vs log(r_tip) should yield slope β ≈ 0.5. For H = 0.3 (rougher), β should be larger (~0.6-0.7) due to increased tip-surface interaction at small scales.

title: Spectral Distortion Metric D_spec
mathematical_formulation:
D_spec = [ ∫∫ |H_true(f) - H_measured(f)|² df / ∫∫ |H_true(f)|² df ]^(1/2)

Alternatively, the Wasserstein distance between normalised PSDs:
D_W = W₂( PSD_measured/||PSD_measured||₁ , PSD_true/||PSD_true||₁ )

Normalised spectral correlation:
C_spec = ∫∫ PSD_true(f) · PSD_measured(f) df / [√(∫∫ PSD_true² df) · √(∫∫ PSD_measured² df)]
physical_interpretation: D_spec quantifies how much the measurement system distorts the surface's power spectrum. Unlike RMSE (spatial-domain scalar), D_spec distinguishes between different types of distortion: low-pass filtering, anisotropic attenuation, and phase errors all produce distinct signatures in D_spec. C_spec measures spectral correlation — how well the measured PSD preserves the shape of the true PSD, even if amplitudes differ.
testable_prediction: D_spec(stylus) and D_spec(optical) will cross at a characteristic spatial frequency f_cross that depends on r_tip, NA, and surface roughness exponent H. C_spec → 0 as either r_tip → ∞ or NA → 0.

title: Morphological Convolution Operator with Finite Tip Geometry
mathematical_formulation:
M_stylus[h(x,y)] = min_{(u,v)∈Ω_tip}[ h(x+u, y+v) + t(u,v) ]

where t(u,v) is the tip shape function (paraboloid approximation):
  t(u,v) = (u² + v²) / (2 · r_tip)  for √(u²+v²) ≤ r_tip · tan(θ_cone/2)

In frequency domain (small-roughness limit):
  H_tip(f) ≈ exp[ -2π² r_tip h''_rms f² ]
  where h''_rms is the RMS surface curvature.
physical_interpretation: The stylus does not perform a simple linear convolution — it performs morphological dilation. The measured profile is the envelope of the tip as it slides over the surface. This is fundamentally nonlinear. However, in the small-roughness limit where the tip radius is much larger than asperity curvature, it reduces to a linear Gaussian filter whose width depends on both tip radius AND surface curvature.
testable_prediction: The effective cutoff frequency f_c ∝ 1/√(r_tip · h''_rms). For surfaces with different curvature but identical r_tip, the measured PSD will differ at high frequencies even with the same instrument.

title: NA–Fidelity Scaling Law for Optical Profilometry
mathematical_formulation:
F(NA, λ, σ) = 1 - exp[ -(NA/NA_crit)^α ]

where:
  F = reconstruction fidelity (0 ≤ F ≤ 1)
  NA_crit = λ / (2 · σ · √(log(SNR)))
  α ≈ 2 (Gaussian optics limit)

Equivalently: SNR_effective = SNR_0 · (NA · σ / λ)^2

Fidelity-bandwidth product: Π = F · BW_effective
physical_interpretation: Optical profilometry reconstruction fidelity F does not degrade gradually with decreasing NA — it follows a threshold behaviour. Below NA_crit, phase information is lost catastrophically due to the inability to resolve surface slopes. The critical NA depends on both roughness amplitude σ and wavelength λ. For typical engineering surfaces (σ ~ 50 nm, λ = 550 nm), NA_crit ≈ 0.05, meaning most commercial WLI systems (NA ≈ 0.3-0.55) operate well above threshold.
testable_prediction: For σ = 50 nm, λ = 550 nm: F(NA) should show a sharp transition near NA ≈ 0.05-0.1. Below this, unwrapping errors proliferate and F → 0 rapidly.
